userPrompt:
Suspense keeps a debug log of what it does, so that a problem can be handed to an agent as files to investigate. It is `suspense.log` in Suspense's own data directory, beside `updates.log`, as the SelfUpdateScope keeps that one, one line per event, each with the time to the millisecond, the project it concerns, and what happened, keeping the last 20,000 lines across sessions.

It logs every child process the application starts, its command, working directory, how long it took, and its exit status, with its standard error when it failed; each task's and question's phases as they happen, queued, spec build, snapshot, preparing the container with its mounts and the podman command, harness started, its first event, each tool call, its result, and the closing snapshot, each with how long it took; each git status refresh, spec build, and language server start or restart, with how long it took; any time the window was unresponsive for more than 200 milliseconds; and every panic, with its backtrace, written before the application exits. It never logs environment variables, credentials, or prompt text. A task's history record also keeps the times of its phases.

The command palette has a "Collect debug info" command that writes a folder, named for the time, in Suspense's data directory and shows it in the file manager: the debug log, `updates.log`, the application's version, platform, and harness report, and the history records of the open project's last ten tasks and questions, with a short README saying what each file is. The palette also has "Open debug log", which opens `suspense.log` as the OpenFileScope opens a file.

We're working in a project whose spec is compiled to .claude/reference, which is where to read it. Each prompt starts with a <task-instructions> block saying what that prompt is for and what it may change. Follow the block at the top of the prompt you are answering; an earlier prompt's block no longer applies.

Its spec's Piton source, in ./spec, is only where edits to the spec go.

Read the spec from its compiled reference under .claude/reference, where inheritance, expressions, and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what `piton slice` prints for it with this harness's adapter.

Never read the .pi source under ./spec to learn what the spec says; that is only where edits to the spec go.

Read only what the change depends on, and start the work as soon as you have. Links to .claude/reference/... in the prompt are the spec for what they name: read those, and then only the pages they link to that the change actually depends on. Don't survey the spec, list its folders, or search it before you start. A page the prompt already gives you as a slice is already read: never read it again. Don't re-read anything you've already read.
instructions:
We're working on both the spec and the code, as a chain. This first step changes the spec only, located in ./spec; the code is changed in the next step.

Write the spec so it describes the application as it should be once the prompt is met, and constrains the code. Once you finish, the spec will be built and the same prompt sent to a coding agent, with your reply, to change the code to match it; so end your reply by saying what you changed in the spec and which anchors the code should follow.

When the work is about Suspense, its modes, its prompts, or its questions, or you are to write a prompt or a question for the user, first read .suspense/suspense-fluency.md once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Suspense works.

Before creating or editing any .pi file, read .suspense/fluency.md once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Piton is written.

Open a .pi file only to change it. Once you have changed the spec, run `piton check` and fix every error it reports, then run `piton build` and check the result in the refreshed reference under .claude/reference, not by reading the source again. Never finish with a spec that `piton check` or `piton build` reports errors in.

Once you have read what the change depends on, and before your first change, write the constraints this task must meet to .suspense/history/1791485622-ImplementDebugInfoCollection.understanding.md, once. Rewrite it only when a constraint in it turns out to be wrong, never after each page you read. It is a Markdown list and nothing else: one line per constraint, at most twelve, each a single short, specific statement of what must be true, written as a link to the compiled reference file it comes from, such as `- [The chain tab has no bottom border in combined mode](.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chain)`. Only list what the spec says; leave out anything you are deciding yourself. Replace a constraint when you learn it was wrong rather than adding another.

End with a reply of a few sentences saying what changed, or for a question, the answer, not a recap of the work or of what you read.

use /lib
from /scope/open-file import OpenFileScope
from /scope/project-data import ProjectDataScope
from /scope/self-update import SelfUpdateScope

export scope DebugLogScope:
    concept: {DebugLogConcept}

concept DebugLogConcept:
    pitch:
        A debug log of what Suspense does, so that a problem can be handed to
        an agent as files to investigate.

    shape: {DebugLogShape}

shape DebugLogShape:
    description:
        The log is `suspense.log` in Suspense's own data directory, beside
        `updates.log`, as the @{SelfUpdateScope} keeps that one. It is one
        line per event, each with the time to the millisecond, the project it
        concerns, by its folder, or none for the application's own, and what
        happened. It keeps the last 20,000 lines, across sessions: each launch
        appends to it, and the oldest lines go once there are more.

    logged:
        It logs:

        \\
        - every child process the application starts: its command, its working directory, how long it took, and its exit status, with its standard error when it failed
        - each task's and question's phases as they happen, each with how long it took: queued, spec build, snapshot, preparing the container, with its mounts and the podman command, harness started, the harness's first event, each tool call, its result, and the closing snapshot
        - each git status refresh, spec build, and language server start or restart, with how long it took
        - any time the window was unresponsive for more than 200 milliseconds, with how long
        - every panic, with its backtrace, written to the log before the application exits
        \\

    neverLogged:
        It never logs environment variables, credentials, or prompt text: a
        command is logged with its arguments but never the prompt given on its
        standard input, nor anything in its environment, and a tool call by
        its kind and the path or command it acted on, never what the harness
        replied.

    phases:
        A task's history record, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says, also keeps
        the times of its phases, as the log names them, when each began and
        ended, to the millisecond.

    collecting:
        The palette's "Collect debug info" writes a folder, named for the
        time, as `debug-2026-10-08-14-03-22`, in Suspense's data directory,
        and shows it in the file manager. It holds:

        \\
        - `suspense.log`, the debug log
        - `updates.log`
        - `about.txt`, the application's version and platform
        - `harness.json`, the open project's harness report
        - `history/`, the history records of the open project's last ten tasks and questions, each beside its hidden anchor's source
        - `README.md`, a short note saying what each file is
        \\

        With no project open, it holds what doesn't need one, and its README
        says no project was open. The palette's "Open debug log" opens
        `suspense.log` as the @{OpenFileScope} opens a file.
EOF
f=spec/scope/palette/index.pi; perl -0pi -e 's/\@\{AboutScope\}, and "Quit"\./\@{AboutScope}, "Collect debug info" and "Open debug log", as the\n            \@{DebugLogScope} says, and "Quit"./' $f; sed -i 's#^from /scope/about import AboutScope$#from /scope/about import AboutScope\nfrom /scope/debug-log import DebugLogScope#' $f
f=spec/scope/application/index.pi; perl -0pi -e 's/(\n    fileOwnership:)/\n    debugLog: \@{DebugLogScope}\n$1/' $f; sed -i 's#^from /scope/container-environment import ContainerEnvironmentScope$#from /scope/container-environment import ContainerEnvironmentScope\nfrom /scope/debug-log import DebugLogScope#' $f
f=spec/scope/project-data/index.pi; perl -pi -e 's/when the task was sent and when it ended, to the millisecond,/when the task was sent and when it ended, and when each of its phases began and ended, as the debug log names them, to the millisecond,/' $f
piton check 2>&1|tail -2; piton build 2>&1|tail -1; ls .claude/reference/scope/debug-log; grep -c "Collect debug info" .claude/reference/scope/palette/index.md

content.text:
I added a new `DebugLogScope` that covers the debug log, `suspense.log`, and the two palette commands, "Collect debug info" and "Open debug log". `piton check` reports no problems and `piton build` wrote 82 files.

**Changes in the spec:**
- **New scope** (`.claude/reference/scope/debug-log/index.md`): it describes the log's location and format, what gets logged, what is never logged, and what the "Collect debug info" folder holds.
- **Palette** (`.claude/reference/scope/palette/index.md`): both new commands are listed.
- **Application scope** (`.claude/reference/scope/application/index.md`): links to the new scope.
- **History record** (`.claude/reference/scope/project-data/index.md#contents`): a task's record now keeps when each phase began and ended, to the millisecond.

**Things I added that you didn't ask for:**
- **Folder name:** the collected folder is named like `debug-2026-10-08-14-03-22`.
- **No project open:** the folder holds only what doesn't need a project, and its README says no project was open.
- **What is never logged:** a command is logged with its arguments, but never the prompt on its standard input or its environment. A tool call is logged by its kind and the path or command it acted on, never by what the harness replied.

**Anchors the code should follow:**
- `DebugLogScope`: `#description`, `#logged`, `#never-logged`, `#phases`, `#collecting`.
- `PaletteScope`: its system commands.
- `ProjectDataScope`: `#contents`.
- `SelfUpdateScope`: `#diagnostics`, for where `updates.log` lives.
- `OpenFileScope`: for "Open debug log".
